utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As the court will see, Judge Robinson is not here. He is unwell, as indeed he was last week, but he has not recovered. Therefore, he will not be sitting either today or tomorrow, and the Chamber, exercising its powers under Rule 15 bis, will sit as the two remaining Judges, being satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to continue with this case as expeditiously as possible, unless there are any objections. Very well. Mr. Nice, it does, of course, mean - and I should make it plain to all - that the Chamber can make no decisions, of course, only being two, no decisions except those which are absolutely necessary for the continuation of the case during the day. In particular, we won't be able to make any decisions on the submissions we're going to hear about Torkildsen and any other matters concerning the conduct of the case. Judge Robinson will have the opportunity, when he returns, to read the submissions, and the Trial Chamber will then make its decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, no doubt if Judge Robinson has any issues he wants addressed by any parties, he will always be in a position to do that on our return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I say that not just because the record is -- reflects the learned Judge's interest in asking me questions from time to time but in order that the accused may know that those interactions are available at that time. Your Honour, we were dealing -- would it be convenient if we deal with the closing -- the remaining submissions about the financial report and then separately, perhaps after the amici and the accused have said what they want to say about that, then turn to other procedural issues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I referred to it discourteously. I meant the financial evidence as "Torkildsen," Mr. Torkildsen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, who is actually sitting next door to me today, as you may have guessed. I know that when we closed last week on this topic, the accused said he had one sentence more that he wanted to say, but unless I'm dissuaded, I'll just carry on and conclude what I say and we can perhaps return to that sentence and anything he wants to say later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. As I recollect, we were hearing your submissions, and had heard part of them, and you had produced a chart for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It's the chart that's referred to in paragraph 54 of the first report, which is the report that covers Kosovo but also part of the earlier period, and it had been amended to incorporate, in small boxes with round corners, the sources relied upon by Mr. Torkildsen for the various propositions that this chart reveals. I've taken you through the chart in short order but sufficiently for these purposes because the chart reveals a control of the movement of money by the accused. It reveals a control of the way the money was then used to finance the operations which include operations at the heart of these allegations. Your Honour, I don't need to say any more about it than that because I know that the Chamber will have considered and will be in a position further to consider the detail of the report if and when it needs to do so. I had a piece of paper that I've now succeeded already in losing. Just give me a moment to find it. That first report, of course, covers Kosovo but also has a slightly broader reach because it sets out the historical position, and overall, it reveals that the accused, even when president of Serbia and not president of the republic, had control of a republic body, the customs administration, which was used for the provision of money for these purposes, and that's an extremely important piece of evidence. Now, we may have had sentences of evidence to the like effect from live witnesses, but the way the matter is charted here in confirmation of that is of great value. It shows that the accused in his control of the movement and use of money was in a position to and did disregard the laws that applied to federal income and the way it should be dealt with. And of course it shows that those funds were channeled outside normal channels to the Serbian MUP at the accused's order in a way that simply matches completely with the Prosecution account that he was directly in charge of those forces, exercising control over them in a way that would not be regarded as typical of a person in his two positions, either president of Serbia or, later, of the republic. And it's interesting to note, as we can find in the summary of conclusions, I think, of this first report, that in the domestic cases against -- paragraph 13 -- that in the domestic cases certainly involving this accused and others, the accused finds himself linked to people like Sainovic, Milutinovic, Stanisic and Markovic, all names with whom he is linked in relation to the alleged crimes in this court. Now, Your Honours, the report is very detailed. It comes in its two parts, and I don't desire at the moment to go into any detail for it would take too much time, but if the Court has any concerns about matters of detail, I can deal with them, the Court being aware that there was, by the amici, a detailed schedule of issues raised which have been responded to in our response of the 16th of June in great detail, item by item. There's going to be little purpose served and a great deal of time consumed in my running over those in detail. The hearsay point that the amici rely on is a point that can always be relied on in any expert report, and we make the point that expert reports have already been adduced, which rely on the admission of out of court observations and statements by one or other kind of individual. It's no different from that. And indeed, the amici's position that everything has to be given live would simply make of any expert topic an uncontrollably large amount of material that would have to be handled. As I said last week, I rather hope that the issue as to whether Mr. Torkildsen is or is not an expert may now be behind us, but of course what experts do, and what all the experts we've seen so far have done, is to take a very large amount of material to which they apply the expertise that they bring, which includes the expertise of analysis, in order to render it valuable to the Court in a manageable way. If we turn to the second report, and I can deal with that shortly. The second report, which deals with -- specifically with the earlier period, it shows, at a time when the accused was the president of Serbia, the establishment of an economic federation, effectively, involving the republic, the RS, and the RSK, all funded by Serbia under the control of the accused. He was the decision-maker in providing the finance and providing all that came with the finance to those Serb bodies outside Serbia, and of course he made admissions which we rely on and which are produced within the report to that effect. And in our respectful submission, the very nature of the allegations made against the accused in relation to his controlling influence on events in both the RSK and the RS and in the territories of which they were organs makes it inevitable that this evidence must be admissible and must be extremely valuable to the Court. But the way the evidence is presented comes in an ideal form for those conducting inquiries - in part, notwithstanding the adversarial process, this Court is conducting an inquiry in its search for the truth - it provides for an ideal - how did I express it? - an ideal form because at all stages the Court can require of the accused to know what is challenged and why and can, as it may or not judge appropriate, further underlying material to be laid before it. Where matters are not, in truth, in issue but are simply fleshed out by this expert from consideration of an enormous amount of material -- not an enormous but a very large amount of material -- fleshed out over the skeleton that at most will be provided by live witnesses saying, "Yes, I was asked to carry sacks of money here and there," then the Court's in a position to do so, and to ensure that it has the correct evidence it would need. So, Your Honour, can I leave those observations there and return to them when my learned friend the amici may have said what they've said and when the accused has contributed what he may want to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution have set up the basis of their allegation on these financial matters. They have set out the evidence upon which they rely. But issue before the Court today is the admissibility of that evidence supported through Mr. Torkildsen, whether the materials that he produces are indeed admissable in the form that the Prosecution seek to present them. If I can go firstly to the issue of expertise. With the original report, a very brief outline of the expertise of Mr. Torkildsen was filed and we sought clarification as to his expertise because that was an objection reasonably open to the accused as to his status. Since that filing, a far more detailed background of his expertise has been put before the Court. It could well be the case that the Court accepts that expertise, but of interest within the argument on this matter is the fact that it is primarily and principally a background of investigation. And I point that out because that is relevant to the submissions that flow. The Court has to be satisfied that this evidence is evidence upon which it requires an expert witness, that the materials sought to be produced before it fall in within that category of evidence upon which the Court, as the principal finders of fact, requires expertise. The trial process doesn't require expert witnesses to come before it to present their conclusions on a wide variety of matters that are in fact the domain of the Judges, and we have raised the issue as to whether this is a subject that truly requires expert evidence to present findings from that expert witness to the Court. It may well be detailed and complex in the sense that there is a lot of it, but being able to judge and see what there is is something that we submit this Trial Chamber is perfectly capable of doing if the evidence is presented before it. Let's now look, then, at the material itself to see what is sought to be brought before the Court through Mr. Torkildsen. The Prosecution have already referred to the schedule filed by the amici on the 16th of December, 2002, and it is that document which I'm going to be using because it makes a number of points that can be made briefly and succinctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is this the first or the second report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's the second. The schedule does identify what I will call a number of minor matters that are contained within the report which we make observations about, such as the first one at page 5, at paragraph 9. The real context --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is matter of weight, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: About inadequate references. The next one is about a book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. If we go to page 5, paragraph 11, attachment number R1, and I'm at part A of the schedule of objections, we have here interview notes of someone who himself is potentially a witness. Since making this filing, the Prosecution have produced further evidence in which Professor Ognjenovic confirms his interview. Those details were sadly lacking on the first filing. But what is sought to be produced is an interview by Mr. Torkildsen of Professor Ognjenovic. So it's not evidence that the expert has observed from the materials, documents, evidence, but in fact an interview conducted by him in which he then produces the statements made by that potential witness. If it is sought to rely upon this evidence, then it would be far more preferable and in the interests of justice that that professor could be called so that the accused could question him as to his point of view and allegation. And using Mr. Torkildsen in between the two, we in effect have a blocking mechanism. Let's move now to the next point within the schedule part A, pages 6 to 15, paragraphs 12 to 26, of the Kosovo report. This is an excerpt of transcript recordings of interview with Kertes and statements made by Kertes which is produced by Mr. Torkildsen as Exhibit R2. In fact, there are only excerpts of the transcript of interview taken by the OTP. Mr. Torkildsen reviews and extracts and summarises what Mr. Kertes, a potential accused himself - or an accused - has said, and then produces it through his report. Annexed to that as R2B, C, D and E, are four witness statements taken in the domestic - and by that I mean national - criminal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. proceedings which were brought against Mr. Kertes. These are a different category of document from the previous ones. They're not OTP documents or OTP investigative material. Again, what Mr. Kertes said about the matter, if produced solely through Torkildsen, prevents the accused from questioning the maker of the statements upon which Mr. Torkildsen relies and is a blocking mechanism. If we go to the next matter, that is what I would call - page 16, paragraph 27 - the travel records of Mr. Kertes, in the context of this argument one of the minor matters, and the Court can deal with that without extensive oral argument. I'm going to deal with the principal matters on this submission because that is probably where the heart of this debate lies. At pages 17 to 19, domestic criminal charges against Mr. Milosevic and a statement made by him in domestic criminal proceedings on the 1st of April 2001, and a statement taken on the 2nd of April. Statements taken by people other than Torkildsen - Mr. Torkildsen, I'm very sorry - at this time and statements concerning domestic proceedings against the accused are matters upon which this case is not, in fact, based. Mr. Torkildsen reviews and summarises that, and we question what is the purpose of a financial investigator in giving a review and summary of that statement. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but the statements themselves, you say, may be admissible as official court documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They may be, yes. From that perspective, we haven't particularly looked at this matter. We're looking at Mr. Torkildsen's role within it, and we'd query what is the purpose of using an expert in that form merely to review and summarise the contents of what was said. We go to page 20, paragraph 34, the next attachment, R5, the excerpt of the statement of Mr. Zebic, former Deputy Prime Minister of the FRY and Federal Minister of Finance. This was a statement that we noticed was unsigned. Whether the entire statement has been produced is unclear. The language of the statement, any translation of the statement that there may have been. No evidence of confirmation, in fact, by Mr. Zebic of what he had said. And again Mr. Torkildsen performs this role, which is central within this theme of our submissions to the Court, of reviewing, extracting portions, putting it in his report, and effectively that blocks the accused from dealing with any issues with the maker of the statement. And in our submission, this is not a true function of an expert witness. We are back into that area we were in in the Kosovo trial where there were summaries of witness statements. And so many witnesses have passed now and I've forgotten the name of the summarising officer, but we clearly dealt with that issue within that form. I think it was Mr. Curtis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Barney Kelly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Barney Kelly. Mr. Curtis as well. And that is, in effect, what is happening here through Mr. Torkildsen, this time not dressed as an investigator but dressed as an expert. I'm not making here any particular point as to whether an investigator cannot be an expert, but I point out to the Court that that is in essence what is happening with this material. If we move on to the next attachment, R6, page 20, paragraph 35. This is Mr. Sainovic's interview, the former Deputy Prime Minister of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And this is material that arose from his own national criminal proceedings and a statement made by him within that context. This isn't a statement taken by Mr. Torkildsen and the OTP, as has been the case in some of the previous attachments, but this is Mr. Sainovic's statement in his national investigation. Again, that evidence of what Mr. Sainovic has said in clearly a position where he would be serving his own self-interest and maybe only too happy to make statements that are untrue about someone else, and I don't know whether that's so or not, but that's the point I make. It's often preferable, if you are going to rely on statements of the co-accused, then you have the other co-accused present to say whether they take issue with that declaration or statement at the time. It makes sense. Here, if this statement was produced through Mr. Torkildsen, again Mr. Torkildsen would only be able to say, quite truthfully, to Mr. Milosevic, "Well, that's what Mr. Sainovic said," and in effect, that would block Mr. Milosevic from ever dealing with Mr. Sainovic and his point of view, and that's why we say that this evidence is not truly the subject of expert evidence. It is really the very usual stuff and essence of trial evidence that the Judges themselves should be able to deal with in observing the questioning of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, given the constraints of time, this is a point which you make -- or these points you make, as I understand it, in relation to a number of other witnesses or witness statements or interviews, over that page and over the next page, that here is effectively evidence being put in in a hearsay form, statements and the like --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- and the right way to do it is, if they want to call the witnesses, Prosecution can do so so that they can be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The roll call goes on: Stanisic, Markovic, Borka Vukic; notes of interview with senior officials from the MUP, Dusan Lalic, Mladen Zinkic [phoen], these are the respective governors or managers of the bank of Yugoslavia; and Mr. Slobodan Raj. And I think the Court has, from our schedule, the specific observations in relation to each of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And they follow the arguments which you have already put to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could come to B, part B. What do you say about that? We have your argument, of course, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Part B, these are the technical side of the presentation largely, where footnotes, references are missing, which in a proper expert's report, the Court, the accused, any expert that the accused may feel inclined to instruct, would be able to check sources. And we've detailed quite a bit of those matters. I don't really want to go into those individually as that will take up too much time, and we've made the points within the schedule. Again, we have again the reports of Radmila Butisin [phoen], Ms. Ljiljana Radenkovic, further examples of statements taken from people within the context of court proceedings where in effect the expert is acting as investigator, summarising evidence. We have made a number of points which are clearly identified. And by example, if I just show that at page 38, paragraph 68, where the expert strays into the role of providing conclusions that are within the remit of the Trial Chamber. That seems to happen quite a lot within these expert reports that we have been asked to deal with in the course of this trial, and we have identified further examples of that. And so what we've done here in part B is provide again specific points where we say, "Well, if this material is to go in before the Trial Chamber, it certainly has to be in a proper form and cleaned up." And I don't mean that disrespectfully, I just mean that it should be more of an entire and full document so that those who want to take issue with it are able to more specifically identify where the sources of Mr. Torkildsen's opinion report are derived from. Again, those are very clear as we've set them out within the table. If we look at page 33, paragraph 60, if I take again, as an example of references and footnoting, Mr. Torkildsen didn't provide references or footnotes to support various statements made by him upon which he was providing what was sought to be relied upon as expert guidance to the Court. And this phrase, "An examination of the banking records reveals that many of the transactions conducted by these eight companies were performed following instructions of Ms. Borka Vukic." Again, if that is something that is to be put forward through the report, those who have to challenge and contest it should be able to see from whence it came to see if in fact the Court, if this evidence does come in, is in fact being given a truly accurate picture. That recurs throughout. I think it would be tedious for me to go through every single one in part B, because I think the points are well made within our document. Does that assist the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want to say anything about the other report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, it comes down to this point of the investigator summarising evidence. It comes down to the same issue and whether this material is genuinely that which should be the subject of an expert giving it before the Court in this form. It's a matter for the Prosecution whether they want to treat this as a part of the evidence against the accused. If they choose to do so and go down that route into what is a very distinct area, then they must bear the consequences in relation to the time and the means by which this should be done. It seemed to the amici that the plea from the Prosecutor was, "We take the view this is essential evidence. We have a conclusion that we would seek the Trial Chamber to draw from it. There is quite a bit of material, dare I say vast amount of material in this context that would have to come within the trial process, and we're seeking this means to achieve that end." The unfairness to the accused is that it may well be that there are constraints of time, and this particular issue which is so important to them, and if it's so important to them is necessarily important to the accused, that he should have the right to challenge, if he chooses to do so, and put his point of view and his case so that the Trial Chamber gets a full picture on the matter. But to use this kind of evidence in this way effectively breaks off and prevents the accused from being able to deal with it specifically, because the investigator, expert, is always able to say, "Well, that's what Mr. Sainovic said. That's what Ms. Vukic says." And when one multiplies that through these extensive reports - we have eight, ten files of it - it becomes a part of the trial that we submit is wholly unsatisfactory, and no one looking back at it would be able to say, "Well, that aspect of the trial was able to be properly dealt with." It's matter for the Prosecution whether they want to rely on it, but in the same way that they stress the importance to them, the importance to the accused has its own reverse indicator. It flows from that in the opposite direction towards him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that here, just like in many other matters, the opposite side has put things topsy-turvy. We're not dealing here with placing any kind of financial documentation in the function of proving some alleged crime and accountability which does not exist but an intentional attempt to make a confusion between what is called economic policy, the economic policy of a particular country, and in this case a country that functioned within the conditions of international sanctions imposed upon it, and the measures for implementing that policy performed by the individual state organs. And I'm going to quote Mr. Nice here. Last time, I think he said the following -- actually, he endeavoured to sidestep the problem of sanctions which were introduced against Yugoslavia. So what? Of course under conditions of sanctions when sanctions have been imposed which were in fact a form of a silent genocide vis-a-vis the 11 million inhabitants of Yugoslavia, another 1.2 million inhabitants in Republika Srpska, and another 300.000 of the inhabitants of Srpska Krajina, this was silent genocide. So under conditions of that kind you could proclaim, for example, that any import or expert was in fact clandestine and a case of smuggling. So what? Isn't it the role of the state organs faced with sanctions to endeavour to do what they can? In order to satisfy Mr. Nice, should they have -- or that other person guiding him -- should we have left our people to die of hunger, to die through lack of medicines, through lack of fuel or anything of that kind? Therefore, there's a confusion here between what is called and what quite obviously Mr. Nice does not know, or perhaps Mr. Torkildsen might be the only person who understands this here because he's the only qualified person in the room, what an economic policy in fact means, the economic of a policy of a country faced with economic sanctions and what mechanisms are through which the state organs implement that particular policy. So that is the difference that cannot be seen here, or rather, intentionally a confusion has been made partially through intent and partially through an absolute lack of knowledge on the part of the matter in question by the opposing side. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Therefore, whether the leadership of a country is striving to solve certain economic problems that it has been faced with, that is one matter and one question, and whether those questions objectively and concretely are solved by the state organs is another question. A moment ago, Mr. Nice mentioned here -- he said or, rather, he enumerated and I made a note of several individuals that he mentioned, one was the vice -- the vice-president for the economy, the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister of the Republic of Serbia, another minister, the fifth was the director of the customs administration. So these were all top functionaries doing their duties and doing their work when Yugoslavia was faced with sanctions. And look at what he says here: 100 million dinars were given to pay soldier reservists in Kosovo and Metohija. So what? Because otherwise, everything relates to 1994 onwards. Those are the dates. And then he goes on to say the following: A large amount of medicines were supplied. Several hundred ambulances and tons of medicines, sanitary material, first aid material and food. They even delve into things like that, he says. Goods were exchanged for other goods. Barter was carried out. And then he says, for example - and this is on page 837 - for instance, he says, for example, on the 30th of April, 1983, Federal Customs Administration drew up an agreement for a compensation with the producers of fuel for the army of Yugoslavia and medicines and food which was sent out to the army of Yugoslavia. So what? Do you think that the leadership of a country, within the frameworks of its economic policy and the Federal Customs Administration, together with the Finance Minister of the federal government, is seeking ways and means to assist the army of its own country? And the fact that we're helping our own army, the army of our own country in this particular way is something that was not done as it should have been, as -- according to the regulations when you're faced with sanctions. And that is something that is -- you are amassing as an important document here. Mr. Kay, a moment ago, said that there was a vast quantity of material and documents, and in that vast quantity of documents and papers, I'd like Mr. Torkildsen, among those thousands of pages, to extract a single one which would indicate my management of any resources, whichever sources they are, to whoever they belong, the economy, the state, whatever. I'd like him to show me one single piece of paper. So economic policy is one thing and it is the competent organs of the state that manage them. Whether it was in keeping with the law and regulations, no, because we were faced with sanctions, so of course not. But Mr. Torkildsen will explain this best to you: In banking transactions, financial transactions, there are always records. There is never any money for which records cannot be found, and there is nobody who deals with money and issues money without receiving a chit, a receipt in return, some written evidence showing what was going on. So I say so what? So what if we helped the army of Yugoslavia? So what if we helped the Republika Srpska or Republika Srpska Krajina? Did the Vatican -- didn't the Vatican assist Croatia, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, goodness knows how many countries? Didn't they help the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina? And so on and so forth. The Germans helped the Croats, the Americans even. And so on and so on. So what if the Serbs assisted the Serbs? Where is there any logic in -- if we did not do so, we would be bastards if we did not help those people during the sanctions, while we were under sanctions. But as it is not my intention to waste my own time or anybody else's time, even the public's time, those who are attending all this, I know that you will deliberate about all these matters exclusively from a formal and legal aspect. I think that the material is quite unsuitable, but, please, just like Mr. Kay emphasised - and I completely agree with him in what he was saying - we have the statement of a -- other persons, I don't want to repeat his enumeration of them, but we have statements of persons to which this evidence relies. And I find it completely unacceptable. They cannot be adopted and accepted and admitted until all those individuals are subjected to cross-examination. Because we don't know how the statements were taken, we don't know whether they were taken in their entirety, and quite obviously, we do know that they were not taken in keeping with the rules and regulations for giving statements, under what circumstances and all the rest of it. And if somebody relies on somebody else's statements, then the person giving the statement must be brought here and subjected to cross-examination and not to take anybody's story for granted, although in addition to all the efforts I have made, I have not been able to find in any of these papers anything that would hold me accountable except that I waged economic policy in the best way I knew how. And might I say that I knew how to do this much better than anybody else, because quite obviously we managed to survive, faced with the sanctions. And how we managed our economy under conditions of sanction will, at a later date in history, be studied as successful defence again the genocidal intents implemented against our nations, and you will be able to see, through the material, that the greatest portion of the resources went to support the economic branches that were having a difficult time, such as the metal industry, the textile industry, and of course, the army and the police and the security of the country, and of course assistance to the Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina, but once again I say so what? This is our own affair. How we're going to spend our own money is up to us. Is there a single document here that has been shown here and that indicates that even one cent was placed in the function of perpetrating a crime of any kind, unless you consider that care and attention to the material position of one's own army or one's own metal industry or one's own textile industry can be considered a crime. Because we found a total collapse of the country under conditions of sanction. So in resisting these measures and resisting sanctions, these are the things we did to survive. So these are all things that have to be cleared up, and none of these statements, not by a single person, can be admitted until that person is brought here for cross-examination. And of course once we receive the final report of Mr. Torkildsen, then Mr. Torkildsen himself will have to take the chair, the witness chair, and be subjected to cross-examination. So that is, in the briefest possible terms, what I have to say about this massive material which I think Mr. Nice has used from his total lack of knowledge. Because had he known anything about all this, he wouldn't have served up this kind of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When were the sanctions imposed, Mr. Milosevic? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sanctions were imposed in 1992. However, those murderous ones and the total blockade, which means when the borders were hermetically closed, that was in 1993, after the Vance-Owen Plan was rejected, even though Yugoslavia wholeheartedly sought to have that plan adopted. Sanctions were imposed upon it because the Assembly of Republika Srpska rejected the Vance-Owen Plan in 1993. And that same year, 1993, Mr. May, as you're asking me, we had soaring inflation because of these horrific sanctions, and the inflation was hundreds of millions of per cent. And then through a very elegant and simple reform, we stopped the inflation in 1994, reduced it to zero and maintained the stability of the dinar, with some minor fluctuations, up to the year 2000. And that will enter into the history of economic policy and economic science as to how we managed to achieve that under those conditions. But that is a separate issue. I am just answering your question, though it is not my duty to answer questions until I take the witness box. But so that you should know, that these sanctions were introduced -- criminal sanctions were introduced in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. As I said at the very outset, you are not obliged to answer any questions, as you point out, but it's sometimes helpful to have matters clarified as we go along, and if you can do so, so much the better. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position of this expert is no different from many other experts dealing with similar lines of work. Forensic accounting experts in commercial or even criminal cases have to review, with their expertise, a range of materials that may be superficially familiar in part, bank accounts and so on, but simply aren't fully understood by the layman and are understood for the purpose of tracing money by the expert. He's undoubtedly an expert and he brings those skills to this exercise. But in any event, as we've explained in our filings in this and I think in other topics, the range of expertise that can assist the Court is broad these days, from the entirely intellectual expert who speaks in entirely intellectual, academic terms, to the practical expert; and inevitably experts will find themselves, in giving evidence, doing a number of things, including exercising their skills in the analysis of documents. That's exactly what this witness has done. A few matters of detail: The Ognjenovic interview was by an investigator called Tore Soldal and also another financial investigator called Rand Sharpe [phoen]. It's no different in form from any other of the many forms of out-of-Court statements that have been admitted in this case. Can we have a very short closed session, please, because I want to deal with propositions in chronological order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused's out-of-court statements were a source, provided a framework or part of a framework that the expert was then able to consider by reference to the documents to see if they fit and support, to see if they go together. They do. That's why each is valuable, the one confirming the other. Zebic's statement has been signed. We've dealt with that. And there's no question of this being a summarising witness. We made it clear that all the documents are available in full when required, so it's not question of summarising their effect. It's looking at out-of-court statements and looking at what documents reveal and seeing the degree to which they match, and they do match. And the Chamber will have seen in relation to a couple of the witnesses that my learned friend Mr. Kay said were inadmissible out-of-court statements, that they don't actually feature in the little square boxes that I've had put on this chart as going to show particular sources of information. Not because they aren't valuable but because they're not critical to particular limbs of the process. So you won't find Sainovic there, and you won't find Zebic there. They provide further supportive material but they're not actually critical to any of those particular lines that we would wish to establish. And of course these are for the most part - because they're made in other jurisdictions - they are declarations against interest, therefore having about them an indicia or indicator of reliability the Chamber can Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. weigh. So far as Slobodan Raj is concerned, his statement you'll find is referred to, and he can be found -- you see where I point. It's towards the bottom left of the statement, there. Now, in one sense his statement is an ICTY statement, I think one of only two ICTY statements referred to in this report, the other one being Ljiljana Radenkovic. His statement, though, is barely an ICTY statement, because he was interviewed and then came back with his own handwritten document which he wished to be annexed to the formal witness statement then taken from him. So it's absolutely his own statement and cannot be subject to any of the particular exclusionary jurisprudence. It's a statement that falls fairly and squarely within Rule 89 and is, in our respectful submission, absolutely appropriate for reference by this expert. My learned friend Mr. Kay's references to footnotes have been dealt with in the Prosecution's document of the 16th of January of this year, and of course there are some ten files of material to which reference can be made and any footnote that may yet be outstanding can always be the subject of an informal request to us and will be dealt with. The suggestion by my learned friend that the accused should have the right to challenge and put his case; precisely so. In having the material assessed in this way, collectively, it is all the easier for him to put his case, or as it would appear, to acknowledge the accuracy of the case presented against him - that seems to be substantially what he was saying - and to reduce to a minimum the amount of further or any live evidence that would have to be called to present this complete picture. Mr. Kay said no one looking back would say that this was properly done. Of course he recognises that to call all the evidence live would be an unacceptable task probably for any Court and wouldn't be undertaken by any Court because it wouldn't be necessary. Without this evidence, looking back simply at the odd word of evidence or the odd line of evidence here or there without an attempt, indeed without the proper execution of the process of analysing the material, would look a dereliction of our duty and, in our respectful submission, would show as a gap on the face of this record. So far as the accused's observations are concerned, his last observation about economic miracle of reform is one that, although there might be indeed a record of some economic turnaround, it's not one that would necessarily be accepted as being to the credit of the accused, and indeed there may yet be evidence to satisfy the Chamber that the accused was concerned -- not just willing but concerned to see the economy in distress because it lent to the power he was able to exercise. And that again shows the need to have economic analysis and expert analysis of what was going on of which this would prove a substantial part. The accused says no document goes to show his control of the money. Maybe no document, but the live evidence matches entirely with the expert analysis and goes to show that what the live evidence says in short form is consistent with what is found. The expert evidence goes to show as well, of course, that there is nobody else revealed on the documents as exercising the power to move this money in illicit ways as was plainly done. Your Honour, the rest of the arguments are, I think, satisfactorily set out in our written pleadings. I'll see if Mr. Torkildsen thinks I've missed anything. But before I ask him that, in our latest filing to which I'm going to turn in just a minute, on witnesses, by error this witness has been recorded as one about whom we make our decision as to whether we regard him as a priority witness later. We do regard him as a priority witness. In our submission, it would be a dereliction of our duties not no to lay before you a full account, as we can present through an expert, of the financial position of this accused and of the organs with which he was associated and which he was in control at the relevant times. Very well. Raj's -- I'm very grateful. The annexed statement of Raj was not handwritten, it was typed by him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The Court will consider these arguments and give our ruling in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I turn, then, to general procedural problems, a topic to which I've been anxious to get since I think before Christmas but for various reasons it hasn't been possible to do so. And if I can make some general observations first, I'll then explain the position through some charts that I've had prepared. Your Honours, it is essential that we bring the Chamber up-to-date with where we are. I see the charts are being distributed. They're going to be I think rather more interesting than I am for the time being but if I could detain you before we turn to them with some observations which I hope will set the position clearly. In conducting this Prosecution, we the Prosecutor have two principles that guide us: First, we must prove the indictments preferred against this accused. Second, we must do everything we can to comply fully with Court orders. It is simply inappropriate for us, or would be inappropriate for us to allow time to run out and then to say, "Well, now we need more time to do our job." That is an inappropriate way for any prosecutor to carry on. And so in a setting where it's been apparent from the beginning that the time limits imposed were - which we of course appealed but unsuccessfully - were bound to be difficult, I have regularly brought the Trial Chamber up-to-date, most recently with confidential filings the essence of which I may touch upon in public now today. We have regularly proposed procedural reforms, and we have, we hope, alerted the Chamber to the difficulties that we collectively face, for, in our respectful submission, disposal of this trial properly is a collective responsibility, we to present our cases and of course for the Trial Chamber to manage the time that is available to this as to other cases. Now, the reality, I think, is that we will in due course have to ask for some additional time. I'm not going to make the application now for this reason: It remains my duty to fit as much evidence as possible within the available time. There remains the possibility of further reduction in our estimates. There remain the possibilities of further important witnesses becoming available whose evidence will be of a density that will mean time may be saved in respect of other witnesses. But inevitably, it will appear, I will be applying for more time, and my expectation is that I will make that application in perhaps a month or so's time when we know where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you on one point. We said that you would have time to cover that which has been lost due to the accused's ill health and rest days. If it's of assistance to you, our calculation at the moment is that about 30 days are outstanding to you as a result of that. We haven't made a precise calculation but it's of that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we may have calculated it in a different way but my feeling is that that's about the same calculation that we've made. When I say we're going to need more time, it's more time beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I say this as well: We have been concerned at all times about the difference between proving a legally sufficient case and proving a complete case, that is, a case where all the most helpful evidence is before you, evidence that we would expect an arbiter of these facts to want to hear from, even if it is not absolutely essential for the legally sufficient or the bare minimum case. I'm going to return to that distinction a little later when we look at the charts. Because of our approach - and I can say this, I suppose, by way of one sentence of indulgence - I suppose I am probably the only person yet charged with the duty of prosecuting an individual who happens to be former head of state in respect of three wars, and you would expect me to find this, and as indeed I do, a challenging and interesting task. In fact, the majority of my time or a great deal of my time is spent in the business of trying to fit - to convert an English phrase to its metric equivalent - a litre into a half-litre jug. The procedure has become, and the timetabling problems have become preoccupying for us. And as a result of that, of course, I have proposed to the Chamber a range of methods by which time could be saved, and it seems to us that none of them has yet found favour, although it has to be said that all of them really amount to concessions by the Prosecution from what would normally be to their advantage, because essentially we have argued in other settings, but I can mention them publicly now, that the appropriate way for getting the maximum amount of evidence into the limited amount of time that is available is by taking evidence in chief in written form in a way that of course is done now by many sophisticated jurisdictions when dealing with judge alone trials of complex civil litigation to which in many ways this litigation is most similar. We have, in making these proposals time and again, we think, reflected, Your Honour -- His Honour Judge May's words about their being something outmoded in the practice of having examination-in-chief orally. Your Honours, can I digress for a second and invite comparison between the speed at which full examination-in-chief and full cross-examination proceeds contrasted with -- and it's not a trial, but something like television programmes that the Court may have seen in the past concerning Yugoslavia, where the proponent of one position speaks his words briefly and the opposite side or another view is given shortly after. Now, we cannot in trials achieve that density of information presentation, and of course although the viewer of a television programme will think at the end of it -- may only last four hours, Death of Yugoslavia only a few hours more. Although at the end of it he may think he has a balanced view, of course there are arguments that he doesn't. But it's our respectful submission to this Chamber that there must be better way of using our time than simply being able to get through witnesses at about the rate, at best, of one a day. And in our submission, the use of more written evidence for evidence in chief and focusing the accused more on what is strictly relevant in cross-examination would enable the Chamber to have more evidence in the limited time available with pointed and relevant cross-examination than is coming our way at the moment. And so although I'm probably wearisome in the number of proposals I've made for attempting to have evidence reduced, wearisome to the Chamber because it imposes on you an obligation to think about it, wearisome to my colleagues who would all prefer, I dare say, the old-fashioned traditional ordinary criminal trial of the United States or England with the opportunities that they give public display of the dramatic and emotional sides of this evidence, despite being wearisome in those ways, what I'm pressing on the Chamber is the absolute need in a case of this kind to maximise the amount of evidence that it can consume. And those of us who, of course, have operated in an environment where evidence goes in in-chief in writing and where cross-examination follows after a limited number of words from the witness, know that the Court's minds are kept working at an optimum and maximum speed for the digestion of the material coming their way and that it is an extremely efficient way of presenting material. My Lord -- Your Honours, we would respectfully make an obvious point about the accused, and that is that he is clearly capable of cross-examining for as long as any witness gives evidence in chief. It is obvious to all that by his doing that he ultimately reduces the amount of time available for other witnesses. The amici generally propose no methods for getting more evidence before the Chamber in the allotted time and seem only to favour the examination rights in the form of cross-examination that reflect, in our submission, a different type of trial from that to which this can most easily be likened. Your Honours, can we just look before the break - because I can explain them at least briefly, at these charts - and can one go on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why does it need to go on the overhead projector?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because people are viewing it so it can then be seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is matter for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at -- the best one to look at first is probably the bottom right-hand chart, because it concerns what's outstanding for Bosnia, and Bosnia hasn't really started very much. On the right is our calculation of the time remaining for Bosnia. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Now, as Your Honour will know from the lists that we provided on Friday, we have divided up witnesses at this stage, and of course provisionally, into two categories. The first category that we regard as essential, priority I witnesses, and the second category, that category of witnesses that I said we judge would make for a complete case. I can give some examples: International negotiators with the accused who, if they were in a position to give evidence publicly would be witnesses we would very much like the Court to hear from; the very senior international military figures, likewise, who could help you. But they are just some of those priority II witnesses. So on the right-hand side, time remaining under our calculation. On the left, in blue, the priority witnesses for Bosnia. If you then go to the top of the blue column, here we we've added in those witnesses whose crime-base evidence is necessary under 92 bis (B) or (D) and on the basis that they have an hour's cross-examination each. Now, before I come to the other two elements in that column, a word about where I've got so far. We have to prove crimes. We can't prove this case simply by linkage. The Bosnia case started out with a very large number of municipalities, and within the bottom part, the 79-odd days has included live evidence for three municipalities for it is down to three municipalities that Bosnia has been reduced. The remaining municipalities that it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just pausing one moment. I think we must adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But let me try and understand the Bosnia position. You're saying that's three municipalities but 79 days of evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The rest is linkage evidence. So that -- so that contains live evidence for just three municipalities, and then all the other municipalities which we would seek to lay before you are under 92 bis (B) or (D) and would occupy, even on the basis of only one hour examination or in reality cross-examination per witness, a total of 31-odd days, 32-odd days. And before I move on, and perhaps I will move on after the break, you can take any examples of these blocks and measure them against the red block and see the consequences for us of the time limit we face. But before -- in case Chamber takes the document away and reviews it generally, the second from left block, priority II for Bosnia, is that category of witness which we think and have always argued would be very valuable for the complete picture. The middle -- the last block, priority V is dealt with in our witness list and is those witnesses whom the Chamber itself indicates it wants to hear from. A very small amount, I think none in respect to Bosnia at the moment, but you'll see in the other chart something for the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can help us perhaps after the adjournment with Sarajevo and Srebrenica, what you propose to do about those particular areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, staying with the Bosnian chart and before I turn to Srebrenica and Sarajevo, the Chamber will recall that originally charged against this accused were allegations in respect of some 47 municipalities. Because of the limitations of time, the reduction has been to three to be proved live, but again on a very reduced number of witnesses, each taking about, I think, a week each or something to that -- a five-day week each. That's Bijeljina, Zvornik, and Bratunac. And in order to provide within the limited time available some appropriate geographical spread, there's only six other municipalities that we seek to prove under the provisions of 92 bis, and that's Visegrad, Foca, Brcko, Bosanski Samac, Prijedor, and Sanski Most, which, therefore, covers the territory to an extent. But this represents an enormous reduction in the case as originally formulated. And so I turn again to the charts. I know, Your Honour, that the Court was concerned that the charts shouldn't be viewed publicly. The Prosecution performance of its duties to the Chamber and to the wider community are a matter of concern and our ability to meet the constraints, our performance in meeting the constraints so far is a matter that, in our respectful submission, could be properly a matter for public consideration and I'd ask that the charts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. This is a matter for us. It's matter for the Trial Chamber that has to manage this case. It's not a public relations exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not intended to be a public relations exercise either, Your Honour. I have throughout, and as the Court knows, been very concerned to help the Court confidentially about our problems, and I'm going to continue in that determination, but the Prosecutor and the Prosecution has not a public relations interest, it has a proper interest in being seen to have done its job properly. Now, Srebrenica and Sarajevo present particular problems. They've each, of course, been the subject of indictments here in respect of other accused, one tried, one awaiting trial completion of a trial. Each of those trials has lasted a very substantial period of time, a year or more. And obviously that type of trial is clearly not possible in the setting of a case like this. They may also be parts of the indictment against the accused that require rather more rather than less evidence, and they have to be seen separately, because, as is revealed in the chart before you, we have prepared a very reduced case that we believe to be legally sufficient against this accused in respect of each of those locations. But even on that extremely reduced basis, Sarajevo we forecast would occupy 20 days, and Srebrenica 21 days. And given that there are only, in our calculation, 70 days remaining from the overall time limit for Bosnia, and given that the priority witnesses for the balance of the Bosnia case, excluding 92 bis, would occupy 79 or 80 days, it's clear that we simply cannot fit all these items into that time. And of course, as I've already explained, if 92 bis is not dealt with in full 92 bis fashion, without cross-examination, there's another 30 days required there. So the Bosnia position before Your Honours is a stark one. It's not entirely surprising, for it is a very large case, arguably the largest of the three. It remains the position that I am doing everything I can - and I'll come back to this in a minute or so - to reduce further that core of 79, 80 days. And it may reduce. Witnesses may not be available. Witnesses may provide more than it was expected, freeing us of the need to call others. But the problem is there. Can I now look back at how we've done? And the Court will recognise to some -- we're obviously doing -- we're calculating on the -- we've centred the calculations in confidential documents that reflect the Court's orders both as to time and as to number of witnesses in order to assess how much time the Court was allowing us for each segment of the trial. And in Kosovo, when the Kosovo section ended on time, it was recognised that there was some outstanding material, and the Chamber was happy with that. And the way we've analysed it, there are a further 11 days required for really category I or priority I witnesses, a couple of days for witnesses that the Chamber wanted us to call, and some seven days or thereabouts in respect of witnesses who, in a perfect world, we forecast the Chamber might want us to call. But let it be noted - I've made this point before and I must make it again - the entire Prosecution evidence in Kosovo in chief occupied about the equivalent of five weeks of an ordinary domestic court's time, and we would urge the Chamber to accept not only the good faith efforts of this Prosecution but that the delivery, the performance to put in a case in chief under conventional, essentially common law procedures in five weeks in chief, in five weeks of court time, is extremely swift. Your Honour will know domestic frauds or customs cases involving one defendant or a couple, in the United Kingdom and in other countries that use broadly this system, can last months. So just 11 more days of priority I witnesses for Kosovo. Croatia, our calculation is that there are about ten more days remaining for Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just help us with the calculation of days. That is the original time limit plus what you estimate you're entitled to because of the time lost through illness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If Your Honour looks at the confidential filings, what we did, in order to understand the Court's rulings and to implement them, was to take the total amount of time that had been allowed as we calculated it and on the basis that when time limits were imposed the accused's medical condition wasn't fully appreciated. We've then taken the number of witnesses the Chamber allowed for each segment of the trial in order to identify the portion or proportion of that overall period of time that the Chamber would have judged appropriate to each segment of the trial, and we have then allocated evidence called as between Kosovo, Croatia, and to the extent Bosnia, and made the appropriate deductions in order to leave us with the conclusion that there is no time left for Kosovo, of course, there are ten days left from this morning for Croatia, and that there are 70 days left remaining for Bosnia. Again, if I may respectfully urge the Chamber to accept this, the Prosecution has, it may be thought, done very well for a conflict as large and detailed as Croatia. There are, in our calculation, 22-odd days of priority witnesses left. So that's ten more days than the time available. But there would be a requirement for 16 days if 92 bis witnesses are to be cross-examined for an hour in the way the Chamber has been minded to do generally, but we respectfully remind the Chamber that in its dealings with Kosovo, it made clear that different considerations could arise as to cross-examination of crime-base witnesses in Croatia and Bosnia from the considerations that affected Kosovo where the accused was raising a particular defence associated with NATO bombing, a defence that of course has no part to play here. And there were several occasions when the Court was quite explicit about reserving its position on whether 92 bis should be full or subject to cross-examination. Now, what we've then done, obviously, is prepared a total picture on our best calculations to date that reflect 80 or 81 days outstanding with -- for all parts of the case. In our judgement, 113 days of priority I witnesses. The same additional 41-odd days for Srebrenica and Sarajevo, with a further addition of 49-odd days for 92 bis witnesses if they are to be the subject of cross-examination. In addition to that, there are four days of evidence, our category V, total priority V witnesses whom the Chamber wishes us to call, and then we've already identified another 33 days of evidence that falls into our priority II witnesses who would make the case complete. Now, Your Honour, this is obviously a very troubling position in which we find ourselves. I repeat, I think, for the third time: Further reductions are being pursued, and further reductions may occur. For example, I can tell Your Honour that you will be receiving today - I hope today - two applications, one public and one not public, to call witnesses who will give central evidence, different in character are the witnesses, absolutely central evidence which should save time. Each of them not being available until now to be added to the list. I can tell you I will have to deal with one of them, I'll deal with one of them at the end publicly because it will help the accused for me to do so. But those endeavours continue. The Chamber will, I'm sure, recognise that one of the consequences of a public trial, as this has been, consequences of many people finding the courage to give evidence publicly has been that more witnesses do make themselves available to us. Frequently valuable witnesses who we can assess as bringing benefit to the potential quality of the judgement and to the saving of time. And we've had a number of witnesses walking in, offering to see us as a result of evidence over the last few weeks, some of them potentially extremely important. And so that in part again explains why I'm not going to make an application for time now, I'm going to see how we go. But, Your Honour, can I press the Chamber to consider the following: The Chamber will remember as well, incidentally, that I have provided you with documents, we called it a fill-box document, it may be a document you'll want to see again, maybe not, but that assesses, as it were, how evidence to date may have met the task imposed on us of proving these counts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We wouldn't discourage you in producing that sort of document. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber will recognise how I have willingly offered my decision-making, in part, to the Chamber if the Chamber ever wanted to involve itself in the decision as to which witnesses it wished to hear from. I recognise the problems with that, but nevertheless, with the case we have to deal with, it's something we'd invite the Chamber to consider perhaps doing at some stage. As things are, the list we've prepared -- and I hope the Chamber had an opportunity to look at the list that was prepared last week, and I'll say a word about that in just a second. As it is, that list has been prepared on the basis of evidence being given in the conventional way because there's no alternative for us at the moment but to assume that that's the basis upon which we're going to proceed and thus, all the time estimates are on that conventional basis, each witness having a summary of the evidence he can give so that the Court an, if it wants to, assess for itself whether these are witnesses who really are witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we can follow the application, if 92 bis is to continue to play its part, effectively you would be asking us to apply that rule to all the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Save in absolutely exceptional circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Save where it doesn't apply, acts and conduct of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Because its consequences for the case as a whole on the time limits allowed are so substantial and because 92 bis was introduced as a rule to enable such evidence to be given in this way. We look -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But we would be treating them as we did the two Dubrovnik witnesses last week. When that effectively happened, they were then cross-examined. General Mangan and Mr. Davies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're obviously at cross-purposes. We're asking that crime-base evidence should be given fully 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I follow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I follow that, of course, but for the remainder of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Full 92 bis. Your Honour has only to look at the overall witness testimony chart to see that 92 bis for the limited number of municipalities, six, that are not to be proved live, the three, and for other 92 bis evidence for Croatia of a crime-base nature, 49 of the remaining 81 days would be consumed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, not at all. And, Your Honour -- so I was -- I was reminding you of the degree to which I've been prepared to surrender my discretion to the broader discretion of the Court in identifying the evidence that's helpful, because I actually -- because it can be urged that that is an appropriate course to take in inquiries of this kind. Because although they're trials, they're also inquiries. But second, or finally, can I propose this: Has the time come for the Chamber now not to be thinking so much in terms of a time bar but to be thinking more in terms of which witnesses it is really essential for the Chamber to hear? When the Chamber made its rulings, time and number of witnesses, it hadn't seen, and I don't think was in a position to forecast, the degree to which this accused would maximise his use of time in cross-examination. The Chamber did in any event not identify fully its reasoning process that led to either the time or the witness numbers. No complaint about that; we've simply done our best to work within those constraints. But it now is impossible. Because our priority -- not our priority. Because principle number one is that we must prove these indictments in the same way as principle number two is that we must do our best to obey all court orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One course we've suggested is reduction in the scale and size of the indictments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, I don't know to what extent you followed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have. From 47 municipalities down to 3 live and six 92 bis to cover, in a representative way, the whole territory of Bosnia, is an enormous reduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Will that be reflected in an amendment to the indictment so that we can follow it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There won't be counts that won't be covered but there will be detail within the counts that won't be proved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And it would be helpful for us to have that in written form at some stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we know where we are exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there hasn't been -- there has been a reduction, as you'll remember, I think, in respect of sexual assaults in Croatia. Several counts have been dropped in respect to that. But in any event, as you'll see - and assuming our calculations are broadly accurate, because we've done our best on the material available to calculate what the Chamber meant by so many days and so much time - we're not actually far short on Croatia in the same way as we weren't far short of delivering in Kosovo. So it could be said, and I wouldn't counter this, that the imposition of time limits served a very useful purpose in making sure that we did get our material in in time. But for this last segment, the problem is it looks too big to solve just by efforts on our part, and particularly given the significant amounts of time that Sarajevo and Srebrenica must take, they being allegations really of a kind that simply cannot be eliminated in any way other than by proper trial and disposal. And so I wonder if the time hasn't come, and I say again I'm happy to keep -- keep battling on to reduce the time, and I'll do that. Has the time come, though, to look at the remaining part of the case in terms of the witnesses to be called rather than just the time bar? And it's for that reason, incidentally, that I've provided you with this list. I said I would say one other thing about this list: Of course the list is provisional and I'm extremely grateful to all these working on this case who put their heads together to prepare it, but it's a jolly useful document for us all to have because we can see where we're going. It will change; names will be deleted and added and the list can be brought up-to-date, but it is essentially a final working document, showing where we're going. It's a document that enables the Court to look ahead and to see which witnesses are coming and to say, "Well, is that witness really going to add to material? Let's see what you've already proved in your fill-box documents. Isn't this duplicative?" And sometimes a hint being -- or a wink being as good as a nod - I never know which one it is - we can take a hint and drop a witness and move on. So because the last thing in the world we want is to find ourselves in any position of irreconcilable disagreement with the Trial Chamber as to the final management of this part of the case, we hope that the tools we've provided you will enable us to plan sensibly for the conclusion of the case, to prove all the counts in an economic way without prejudicing the accused but without prejudicing the Prosecution either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Nice. We will consider the position in the light of this document. There can be no doubt that time limits will remain, but we will consider the difficulties which the Prosecution outline. We will consider whether any amendment to our procedures should be considered, should be unnecessary. And of course, as I said earlier, it's not a matter that we can deal with, in any event, in the absence of Judge Robinson, but he will have the opportunity of reading what you've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, then before I sit down and invite Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff to take the next witness, I said I'd mention one witness in particular. There's a witness we would like to call as early as next Tuesday because of problems with his timetable. We haven't been able to make the application until today -- he's not on the list. We haven't been able to make the application today because he hasn't been freed by the authorities that bind him to give evidence until now. It's a former Ambassador to Croatia called Peter Galbraith. You've heard him mentioned. His name's within the transcript. He can provide very valuable evidence. We should be in a position to serve a summary today, and I hope to be able to comply with all our other disclosure duties today or tomorrow. I'm not asking for you to make a decision about that because, of course, you can't in the absence of Judge Robinson, and you can't without having, I think, a paper document before you to deal with, but I've given the earliest possible notice I can to the accused. I forecast a written application that will come I hope today, and we will be inviting a foreshortening of all the time limits to enable him to be called on next Tuesday. That application will come together with another application which I think will bear a pseudonym of an extremely important witness whose evidence will add materially to the evidence before the Chamber and also save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. It's not for you to comment on the conduct of the Prosecution case insofar as it's been related today. It's a problem for them. We are not going to deal with any application in relation to the witnesses. We will get it in writing, and we will hear from you in due course on it. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. No, Mr. Milosevic. There's nothing relevant for you to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have something relevant to say. It's not a question of the technique of the presentation of so-called evidence but certain principled positions and absurd allegations that we have heard here, and I assume I'm entitled to respond to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. It's a matter for the Prosecution. It's between the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber as to how they manage their case. If there is a change in our procedures, which is proposed, such as having all the witnesses give evidence in the form of statements, before we take such a course, you will have the opportunity to address us upon it. But at the moment, we're not in a position to make such a decision and we haven't done so, so there is no application at this stage which is before the Court on which we need you to address us. But as I say, should the time come when we intend to take up any of the suggestions or we want to consider any of the suggestions made by the Prosecution which affect the giving of evidence, we will allow you to call -- to address us on it, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. But would you be kind enough to give me an explanation then, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Depends what it's about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We heard Mr. Nice saying that the collective task here is to prove the allegations in the indictment. I had believed that the task of any legal court in the world is to prove the truth. And even in view of the position held by the so-called Prosecution, they should be obliged to try and establish the truth rather than to prove the allegations in the indictment. Because we heard a number of absurdities. A moment ago Mr. Nice even said that the sanctions of the international community suited us. That can only be compared with the -- another absurd statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, time is short. If there was a general point -- if there was a general point, something we were going to consider which would affect your position, we would give you the opportunity to address us, but right now we're going to go on with the evidence. Time is short, and we will hear evidence and begin with Mr. Grujic, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is he here? No, Mr. Milosevic. You are attempting to make a speech. Yes. Let's go on with Mr. Grujic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this is not a speech. I am referring to what we heard with respect to this rather extensive submission of the opposing side regarding their proposal for formal acknowledgement of adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to decide on that today or indeed at any time without argument. Before we admit any evidence like that, you'll have the opportunity to address us. And I can tell you that for the moment, we're going to go on dealing with the Croatian evidence, and we've got all the 92 bis witnesses to consider first before we go on to deal with adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Senior Legal Officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have the witness. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Please -- Mr. Grujic, please state your name for the record, your name and profession. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Please state your name and profession for the record.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: [In English] Translator no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
